children: India’s efforts to build a domestic battery cell manufacturing industry have not gathered pace more than five years after an ₹18,100-crore incentive scheme was launched to establish 50 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) capacity.

The production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme was designed to reduce import dependence by incentivising large-scale manufacturing and domestic value-addition. The selected manufacturers were required to achieve at least 25 per cent domestic value-addition initially, rising to 60 per cent over five years.

Of the targeted 50 GWh manufacturing capacity, 40 GWh was awarded in two rounds to four beneficiaries: Ola Cell Technologies; Reliance New Energy Battery Storage; Reliance New Energy Battery; and ACC Energy Storage (Rajesh Exports). The remaining 10 GWh capacity was later put up for fresh bidding. The second allocation of 10 GWh to Reliance in 2024 did not help meet the programme’s capacity target, prompting another tender.
Progress, however, has been slow. In February, the Ministry of Heavy Industries said only 1 GWh of the 40 GWh awarded had been installed, at Ola’s facility in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu.

The plant began pilot production in March 2024 and was working towards stabilising operations for commercial production. No beneficiary had claimed an incentive under the scheme, according to the ministry’s reply to Parliament.

The issue needs to be understood within a context, says Ankur Khaitan, MD and CEO, TACC Ltd, a subsidiary of HEG Advanced Materials, which develops carbon and graphite products for energy storage and industrial applications. “Cell manufacturing is one of the most technically complex industries, and India is building it from scratch,” Khaitan says.

He points out that several external factors have slowed the industry, including restrictions on the export of critical equipment and knowhow from key global hubs, and a sharp fall in global cell prices, which has raised the bar for new entrants.

There is heavy import dependence for the active materials anode and cathode, which account for over 60 per cent of the cell’s cost. “Until that layer is built domestically, Indian cells will carry an import cost base, no matter how well the lines run,” says Khaitan.

Agreeing with him, Vinay Rustagi, Chief Business Officer, Premier Energies Ltd, says the best option to get around these challenges could be the adoption of new technologies like sodium ion. But he also stresses that “commercialisation of new technologies is a costly and time-intensive process”.
That said, significant investments have been announced; “several players have moved from construction to commissioning,” observes Khaitan.

Projects worth 178 GWhr have been announced outside the PLI scheme. So, the battery cell industry in India is delicately poised — little track record but lots of hope. Experts note that patient capital and consistent policy support are key factors for growth.

In July, the Ministry of Heavy Industries, which administers the ACC PLI scheme, issued a tender calling for manufacturers to establish capacity for large battery systems to support renewable energy integration and grid balancing.

The tender has raised questions over the transparency of the bidding process. In its roughly 90-page response to pre-bid queries, the ministry relied heavily on standard replies. Of 265 queries, 261 reportedly received stock responses, including “The relevant provisions of the bid documents are self-explanatory” and “Provisions of the bid documents shall prevail”.

For example, in a query related to vanadium redox flow batteries, the bidder wanted to know whether the ‘cell’ referred to individual cell, stack, module or integrated system, whether Indian manufacture of key components and processes such as electrolyte preparation meets the domestic value-addition requirement, and whether technology-specific testing methods could be used where prescribed tests are unsuitable.
It is a moot point whether a potential bidder who is confused about “relevant provisions of the bid documents” will submit a bid at all.

The deadline for the bids, initially October 13, has been extended to November 10, with technical bids scheduled to open on November 11. The government has not given any response, but industry sources say the deadline extension was due to poor response.

title: Dull battery cell manufacturing a blot on India’s renewable energy growth story
